description.narrative:
In a region where securing Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights (SRHR) is especially challenging, Masarouna will mobilize the power of young people’s collective action in six Middle East and North Africa (MENA) countries to support their fight for greater freedom of choice and respect for their SRHR through new and innovative pathways for change. Our vision is that young people (YP) meaningfully induce sustainable change that will enable them to enjoy their SRHR. Lebanon is one of the countries where the Masarouna programme will be implemented.
Context: In 2019, 41.4% of MENA’s population was aged 15-39, making it one of the world’s youngest regions. In recent years, young people have demonstrated their ability to become main drivers for changein response to long-standing structural inequalities, rising authoritarianism and increased levels of conflict and fragility. Young people in MENA continue to facesome of the most vocal conservative opposition to their SRHR. The problem that Masarouna will tackle is the perpetual obfuscation and the increasing weaponization of SRHR as a form of social control. This strips SRHR of the urgency it deserves, yet, we strongly believe fulfilling young people’s SRHR can have a transformative effect on sustainable development due to its connection with basic human well-being and gender equality. Strategic objective: Young people in six selected countries in the MENA region achieve more freedom to enjoy their SRHR in inclusive societies. Targeted group: Young people aged 18-35, in particular (unmarried) women and LGBTQI+. Activists and individuals will be mobilized as agents and drivers of change throughout the programme cycle.
The programme’s strategic objective and outcomes contribute directly to achievingSDGs 3 (health and well-being), 5 (gender equality) and 10 (reduced inequalities. The programme is fully aligned with the ICPD25 Nairobi statement’s call for renewed commitments towards women’s and YoungPeople’s SRHR.
The Masarouna programme implementstwo main pathways of change:
1: Lobby and advocacy with young people for their SRHR The first pathway promotes greater accountability of governments to adhere to international SRHR standards, human rights frameworks and agreements; promotes young people’s active and meaningful involvement in policy agenda-setting and decision-making; and increases public awareness on SRHR, including through media engagement, aiming to create new narratives on SRHR.
2: Strengthening civilsociety and reinventing civic space A strong civilsociety can be a mobilizer, an amplifier of voices and a watchdog. With strengthened capacities, CSOs can create a sense of urgency around SRHR to push for sustainable change. CSOs need the space to play this political role, whichMasarouna aims to reinvent by promoting the political activation and participation of young people and creating andstrengthening alternative civic spaces, both online and offline. Working online allows for reaching young people at scale by circumventinggatekeepers and mitigating risks around censorship.

participating-org.narrative: Oxfam has been working in Lebanon since 2006; it has a regional Gender Justice Hub that administers a regional gender justice programme and a Lebanon programme that focuses on three thematic areas of work: Humanitarian, Economic Justice, and Active Citizenship <(><<)>(><(><<)><(><<)>)>(><(><<)>(><(>&<)><(><<)>)><(><<)>(><(><<)><(><<)>)>)> Governance. Over the course of the past three years, Oxfam in Lebanon has integrated its humanitarian and development programming into a #one programme approach#, as described in the Oxfam Country Strategy. The humanitarian component of the strategy looks at the continuation of life-saving WaSH service provision, protection services and cash assistance, while in parallel the development programs, in collaboration with local authorities and civil society, aim to address the underlying root causes of inequality and poverty over the longer-term, including through policy change. Our vision is that, by the end of 2021, marginalized women and men (Lebanese, Palestinian and Syrian populations including refugees)are protected and empowered to enjoy their basic rights, enabling them to live in dignity within a more equitable society. Oxfam inLebanon has a main office in Beirut, and two operational offices in Zahle (Bekaa governance) and Tripoli (North governance).

Compared to other countries in the region, the digital space is open and free, but the economic crisisis limiting accessibility and digital services

Update Oct. 2023 RNW Media's partner will strengthen its platform - a community based membership program - which enables audiences to find safer spaces for self expression and access to information. Through becoming a member of "the platform", communitymembers will have the chance to engage in trainings on human rights topics which eventually allows further engagement in policy and practice changes on SRHR, as well as, members of the platform are encouraged to engage with the editorial team to share their feedback, needs and suggestions through monthly open sessions. Oxfam is currently conducting a baseline study to assess the dynamics of civic space in the country and will include context-specific, community-specific information to define "civic space" in a way that makes sense for partners. Oxfam in country had so far not defined its 5-year target for this KI; at midterm, it is setting itat 2 cases. RNW Media is not adjusting its 5-year for this KI at midterm, keeping it at 1 case. The consolidated target was adjusted from 1 to 2 cases (all other levels) at midterm, for which we took the highest target between the consortium partners (Oxfam #2, RNW Media #1), to avoid possible double counting in the case of collective action.

KI-1a # Governmental policies blocked, adopted and/or improved to enable diverse young people to enjoy their SRHR

comment.narrative: There are no clear national laws, programmes, policies, plans, or procedures related to SRHR integration, even though the country has adopted/endorsed international commitments and ratified important international treaties related to SRHR issues. On a regional level, the country ratified several Arab legal frameworks; however, the actual implementation and protection mechanisms are weak and ineffective. One main obstacle in coming to national legislation on many SRHR matters is that there is no unified civil law for personal status in the country. Citizens and residents are subject to the sectarian laws. Added to the absence of national legislation, political leadership and will to prioritize SRHR is low. SRH care is not covered by public or private health insurance, making it difficult to access for all but a privileged few. Government attempts at silencing Gender and Bodily Rights Defenders are also observed.

New Oct 2023: One Oxfam Masarouna partner will draft a governmental policy paper, which will be a tool to campaign and advocate for the rights of youth in their communities, and to disseminate knowledge and information on SRHR in universities, schools, and hospitals. Youth will be among the main participants in producing the paper along with academics, organizations’ representatives, and frontline health providers. (The indicator and 5-year target were included at midterm)

description.narrative: KI-1b # Governmental policies enabling diverse young people to enjoy their SRHR that are better implemented or enforced

On a regional level, the country ratified several Arab legal frameworks; however, the actual implementation and protection mechanisms are weak and ineffective. One main obstacle in coming to national legislation on many SRHR matters is that there is no unified civil law for personal status in the country. Citizens and residents are subject to the sectarian laws. Added to the absence of national legislation, political leadership and will to prioritize SRHR is low. Sexual health care is not covered by public or private health insurance, making it difficult to access for all but a privileged few. Government attempts at silencing Gender and Bodily Rights Defenders are also observed.

There hasn't been yet any implementation in that regard, hence no better enforcement of any policy.In 2023, a partner was identified and selected, ideation of concept note was finalized and partnership assessment was conducted by Oxfam. This partner willbe working on producing a policy paper, which will enable diverse young people to enjoy their SRHR. Moreover, civic space mapping is currently in progress, with the aim of producing a report to inform our advocacy efforts. The aforementioned preparatorysteps will set the ground for the work on governmental policies better implemented or enforced.

Update Oct. 2023: Considering the current unstable situation in the country (political, backlash, security), Oxfam may be unable to achieve the initially planned target of ''1'' governmental policies better implemented or enforced. Therefore we have changed the 5-year target to zero at midterm. Throughout the remaining 2 years of implementation, we will try to progress towards such change, but are unsure to achieve actual policy change.

description.narrative: KI-16 # CSOs/movements, both women and youth led, engaged in Masarouna

comment.narrative: The Oxfam Country Office joined the Masarouna programme in 2022, together with consortium partners SMEX and Fe-male, and the strategic partner, all 'both women and youth led" organisations. The strategic partner brings to Masarouna a wealth of expertiseon SRHR in the Arab world. Fe-Male, as a regional feminist collective working in MENA, strengthens the feminist focus of Masarouna and works with women and girls to eliminate injustice through building a young feminist movement, empowering agents of change, and campaigning together against discriminatory norms and policies SMEX has extensive experience and expertise on advancing digital rights in the country and the Arab region through research, campaigns and advocacy that encourages users to engage critically with digital technologies, media and networks. With a growing online civic space and challenges around safeguarding it, a focus on online human rights violations and digital rights will provide a major contribution in reaching the Masarouna objectives. Beyond the consortium partners and strategic partner, the baseline and partner scoping will define the in-country strategy and selection of new partners in the country for 2022 and beyond. Baseline Information will be added once partners are selected.

During 2024, 2 CSOs and 9 informal movement/groups were engaged in Masarouna along with Oxfam in country in the category "both women and youth led". 4 informal groups had their implementation completed by the end of 2024 while the other partners will continue their activities in 2025. Additionally, Oxfam in country engaged with FEMALE, the consortium member, during 2024. However, the partnership between Oxfam and FEMALE is not counted in the quantitative info to avoid double counting as we report the engagement of FEMALE on the regional/global level.
FEMALE continued engagement with their "both women and youth led" partner in 2024 in the form of capacity building training.
SMEX engaged with two both women and youth led organisations in country; with one of them, the partnership concluded end of 2024; and with the other, there is an ongoing partnership till mid 2025.

In 2022, the Oxfam Country Office, consortium partners SMEX and Fe-Male, and the Masarouna strategic partner, joined the Masarouna programme and were still working to identify and select local partners to work with from 2023 onwards. (For the quantitative actual, only the Oxfam Country Office is included in the IATI report, as the other three organisations are also working at and included in the IATI report at Regional-Global level.)

Oxfam in the country signed an agreement with 1 both women and youth led organization and started the selection process for informal movements to be granted group cash transfers in order to support in various SRHR initiatives. The partner will engage with young people to develop a policy paper which will serve as a tool to advocate for YP's SRH rights and will also train YP to raise awareness on SRHR among their peers in their community. FEMALE selected a subgrantee in 2023, which is a national group working in rural areas with girls and women to raise awareness on SRHR topics. In 2023, the partnership between Oxfam in country, consortium partners SMEX and FEMALE, and strategic partner evolved through co-creation and mutual capacity building opportunities such as learning events and expertise exchange.(For the quantitative actual, only Oxfam is included in the IATI report for the country, as the other three organisations are also working at and included in the IATI report at Regional-Global level.)

During the course of the project, the partnership between consortium partners in the country will be established and strengthened as the partners get to know each other and each other's strengths better. The partnership will evolve through co-creation and mutual capacity building opportunities such as learning events and expertise exchange. (For the quantitative target, only the Oxfam Country Office is included in the IATI report, as Fe-Male, SMEX and the strategic partner are also working at and included in the IATI report at Regional-Global level.)

During the course of the project, the partnership between consortium partners in the country will be established and strengthened as the partners get to know each other and each other's strengths better. The partnership will evolve through co-creation and mutual capacity building opportunities such as learning events and expertise exchange. The Oxfam Country Office will embrace a polyculture nature of engaging with diverse and wide range of local and national responders (e.g. private sector/organizations/think tanks/unis/ women-led and youth-led CSOs) to strengthen organizational capacities but also work with them to promote young people's SRHR and promote an open civic space in the country. description.narrative: KI-16 # Women led CSOs/movements engaged in Masarouna

comment.narrative:
During 2024, Oxfam in country engaged with 1 women led CSO/subgrantee and 17 informal groups. 16 of the informal groups agreements ended by December 2024. However, Oxfam will continue providing capacity building for these groups and registered organizations.
SMEX engaged with one women led organisation, with whom they will have an ongoing partnership till mid 2025.

Up until now, 5 women-led CSOs confirmed their interested in working with Oxfam in the country under Masarouna, but Oxfam is still finalising its partnership mapping phase and more partners might join the program in future. The role of the identified partners will be to work on drafting a policy paper and on capacity strengthening of young people to advocate for SRHR.

Up until now, Oxfam is working with 3 women-led CSOs and is in the process signing agreements with 14 other women led organisations in the near future. Throughout year 5, Oxfam will be selecting and working with 6 additional informal groups who will be granted group cash transfers for implementing SRHR initiatives, in addition to local CSOs (type and number to be defined) as Oxfam will launch a call for application for subgrants in November 2024.

description.narrative: KI-16 # Youth led CSOs/movements engaged in Masarouna

comment.narrative:
During 2024, 3 youth-led CSOs and 13 youth-led informal movements were engaged by Oxfam: 1 partner, 2 subgrantees and 13 informal groups. 9 of the informal groups had their projects ending in December 2024 while the others continue the implementation in 2025. Oxfam will continue providing capacity building for these CSOs during 2025.
FEMALE engaged with 2 youth led CSOs in country, providing capacity building and a subgrant to support their advocacy work.
A youth led organisation which participatedin the Strategic Partners Advocacy Lab in 2023 - remained engaged in 2024, and finished their projects post march 2024. They stopped being engaged after their program implementations were complete. The Strategic Partner continued its partnership with another youth-led initiative, which continued to actively contribute despite the challenges faced by other partners (this partner is not counted again, as already counted for Oxfam).
SMEX engaged with youth led organisation in country, with whom they will have an ongoing partnership till mid 2025 (this organisation is not counted again as it is one of the informal groups that Oxfam engaged with as well).

In 2023, Oxfam in the country signed an agreement with 1 youth-led organization. The youth-led organization program will provide capacity building for caregivers and professional about YP SRHR, and will also provide awareness sessions and trainings to youth about SRHR. Their program will also create a digital safe space for young people to get accurate SRHR information and discuss about SRHR topics in a confidentiality.
In 2023, the strategic partner engaged a youth led organisation operating in the country, in their Advocacy Lab.

1 youth led CSO and 1 youth-led movement identified by Oxfam in the country will work on digital SRHR and will provide capacity building to health professional and caregivers on SRHR. Also, Oxfam is currently in the process of selecting additional informal groups to implement initiatives related to civic space and/or SRHR.

Up until now, Oxfam is working with 2 youth-led CSOs and is in the process of signing agreements with 9 more youth-led organisations. Throughout year 5, Oxfam will be selecting and working with 7 additional informal groups who will be granted group cashtransfers for implementing SRHR initiatives, in addition to local CSOs (type and number to be defined) as Oxfam will launch a call for application for subgrant in November 2024. The Strategic Partner's youth led partner will no longer be engaged in 2025; new partners still to be identified.
